2. Serve at once in its leaf, with grated coconut alongside. Cold bibingka is merely cake; hot, it is Christmas.

recipes.name: Puto

items.name: Cheddar cheese
items.description: 60 g, in small flat strips for the caps

items.name: Salted duck eggs
items.description: 1, sliced, for some of the caps

recipes.description:
Puto appear beside dinuguan as if by law: little white steamed cakes whose sweetness answers the dark, savoury stew. They ask only two things of you — a rested batter and a steamer lid that does not drip.

## 1. Mix, then rest

1. Whisk the rice flour, sugar, baking powder and salt, then whisk in the coconut milk and water until completely smooth and thin.
2. Rest the batter for 30 minutes. Rice flour drinks slowly; skip the rest and the puto come out gritty.

## 2. Rig the steamer

1. Set the steamer over a gentle boil and wrap the lid in a tea towel, corners tied up at the handle. This is not optional — condensation dripping from a bare lid craters the glossy tops.
2. Grease your moulds: puto tins, mini muffin tins or silicone cups all work.

## 3. Steam in batches

1. Stir the batter, fill the moulds four-fifths full and steam over medium-gentle heat for 8 minutes.
2. Lay a strip of cheese, or a sliver of salted egg, on each cake and steam for 2-3 minutes more, until a toothpick comes out clean. Keep the steam gentle: fierce heat splits the tops.
3. Rest a minute, loosen with a thin knife, pop them out and repeat with the rest of the batter.

## 4. Serve

1. Pile up and serve warm — beside dinuguan if it is lunch, with coffee if it is merienda. The sweet-against-savoury pairing is the whole point, and nobody has improved on it.

recipes.name: Turon

items.name: Saba bananas
items.description: 6 ripe, halved lengthways (saba; plantains at a push)

recipes.description:
Turon is the smell of three in the afternoon: banana and caramel drifting off a street cart, announcing merienda to the whole neighbourhood. What separates a lacquered, crackling turon from a merely fried one happens in the oil, not the wrapper.

## 1. Roll

1. Roll each banana half in the brown sugar until well coated.
2. Place a banana half near one corner of a wrapper, lay a strip or two of jackfruit along it, fold in the sides and roll tight, sealing the last edge with a wet fingertip. Tight matters — trapped air balloons in hot oil.

## 2. Fry into lacquer

1. Heat 1-2 cm of oil in a wide pan over medium heat. Sprinkle the sugar straight into the oil and wait until it melts into amber streaks. The sugar goes into the pan, not only onto the banana — this is the entire trick.
2. Lay the turon in seam down and fry, turning, for 3-4 minutes a side, spooning the molten sugar over so it nets onto the wrapper and hardens into deep amber glass.
3. Mind the heat: caramel goes from lacquer to bitter in about a minute of inattention.

## 3. Drain and serve

1. Lift onto a wire rack, never onto kitchen paper — the caramel welds itself to paper.
2. Wait 5 minutes, because the filling is molten, then eat standing up, mid-afternoon, as intended.

recipes.name: Ginataang bilo-bilo

items.name: Water
items.description: 160 ml for the dough, 400 ml for the pot, plus a pan-full to boil the sago

items.name: Coconut cream
items.description: 200 ml, stirred in at the end (kakang gata)

recipes.description:
Ginataang bilo-bilo is what rainy afternoons are for: a warm, sweet coconut stew of chewy rice balls, sago and fruit, assembled from whatever the cupboard holds. The bilo-bilo carry their own timer — they float when they are done.

## 1. Cook the sago

1. Boil the sago in a pan-full of water, stirring at first so the pearls do not clump, for 15-20 minutes until translucent with only a pinprick of white at the centre. Turn off the heat, cover for 10 minutes to finish, then drain and rinse under cold water.

## 2. Roll the bilo-bilo

1. Mix the glutinous rice flour with the dough water into a soft, pliable dough that no longer sticks to your palms.
2. Roll into marble-sized balls and keep them under a damp cloth. This stage traditionally goes to the children, which is why half the country believes it learned to cook during a typhoon.

## 3. Build the pot

1. Bring the coconut milk, the pot water, the sugar and the salt to a gentle simmer in a wide pan. Never let it boil hard — coconut milk punished with high heat splits into oil.
2. Add the sweet potato and simmer for 8 minutes, then the saba, and simmer 5 minutes more.

## 4. The balls set the timer

1. Drop in the bilo-bilo one at a time. They sink, then bob up as they cook through: floating means done, no clock required.
2. Add the drained sago and the jackfruit, stir in the coconut cream and warm through without letting it boil.

## 5. Serve warm

1. Ladle into bowls while the rain keeps going. It thickens as it stands; tomorrow, loosen the leftovers with a splash of coconut milk and call it a second merienda.
